newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel phone competition to start in seven months.
newsitem.headline: Israel phone competition to start in seven months.

text.p: The two winning consortia for licences to operate international phone services in Israel will begin operations in about seven months, the Communications Ministry said on Wednesday.

"The companies are expected to begin operating within six months after they receive their licences," which will be in about 30 days, Shlomo Wax, the ministry's director-general, told a news conference.
The first winning group includes Italy's STET, SBC Communications (formerly Southwestern Bell) ; Aureq Group (a joint venture between SBC and the Israeli Kahan Group); Israel's Globescom, and Kahan.
The second is led by Clalcom, a subsidiary of Clal Industries and includes Sprint Corp ; Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom, and Israel's Matav Cable Systems Media Ltd.

Communications Minister Limor Livnat called the tender an important step in opening up Israel's telecommunications market. "It will lead to a real revolution," she said. "It's just the first step in a total opening up of the local telecommunications market."
She said the ministry would be taking bids for a third operator for the mobile phone market and was weighing plans to open up the domestic telephone market to competition within the next four years.

The international phone service tender marks the latest step in the government's policy of whittling down the telephone monopoly of state-owned Bezeq Israel Telecom. Mobile phone service was opened to competition in 1994, when a licence was awarded to the Cellcom consortium to compete with a joint venture controlled by Bezeq and Motorola.

Wax said the entry of two contenders in international phone service will lead to a sharp drop in rates. For instance, he said, the two winners are committed to charging tariffs of 0.62-0.65 shekel a minute for a call to the United States at peak hours, compared with Bezeq's current rate of 3.53 shekels.
He noted that 50 percent of the decision on selecting the two winners was based on tariffs.

Although Bezeq stands to lose a big chunk of the $700 million international calling market, that will be partly offset by interconnection and user fees the two new operators will have to pay it. A third of Bezeq's revenues and nearly half of its profits derive from international service.
Wax said subscribers would be able to freely choose among the three operators and change companies easily and cheaply.

The two consortia have promised to invest $100 million over the 10-year life of their licences. The licences are renewable, but the government is permitted to offer additional licences in the year 2002.

Mair Laiser, chairman of the Clalcom-led group, estimated the consortium would invest 400 million shekels in setting up the group. He said his group's strength was that its partners specialised in complementary fields of voice, data and cellular communications and cable.
